So far every track has held MIDI notes. An **audio track** holds sound: what a microphone heard. Recording one is simple
(pick the track, press record, play), but the microphone hears *everything* in the room, including the song you are playing
along to. This lesson records twice, once with speakers and once with headphones, and measures the difference.

You need a microphone (the one in a laptop or a headset is fine), Chrome or Edge, and a pair of headphones.

## The setup

The **Voice** track below is an audio track; the band has 8 bars of drums, bass and keys to play along with. With the Voice track
selected, the **● Rec** button records from the microphone: a short sound check first (it tells speakers from headphones and asks
for your loudest phrase), then one bar of count-in, then recording. The small meter by the buttons is the microphone's **input level**:
keep your loudest moments out of the red ([Recording 1: Gain Staging](rec-gain-staging.qmd)).

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-record" data-preset="record" data-show="transport tracks editor mixer record"></div>

## Experiment 1: speakers

1. Take off your headphones and play the band through your speakers at a normal listening level.
2. Select the **Voice** track, press **● Rec** and **stay silent** for the whole 8 bars. Press Space to stop.
3. Under the tracks, *This take* gives the take's **average level**. Write it down: everything in that take is **bleed**,
   the band and the click coming back into the microphone.
4. Click **S** on the Voice track to solo it and play. You hear the band, thin and roomy, and the click.
5. Now record yourself singing or clapping along. Solo it again: you, *plus* the band, *plus* the click.

Why it matters: that copy of the band is now part of your vocal for good. Turn the vocal up and the band comes up too.
Change a chord in the keys part, and the old chord is still faintly in the vocal. Compress or EQ the vocal and you
compress and EQ the band in it. And the click, which nobody is meant to hear, is in the song.

## Experiment 2: headphones

1. Plug in headphones, put them on, and **record 8 silent bars again**.
2. Compare the average level with the speaker take. Closed headphones at a sensible level are usually **20 to 40 dB** quieter in
   the microphone: almost nothing.
3. Now turn the headphones up loud, or take one side off, and record silence again. Headphones leak too: open-back ones,
   loud clicks and a mic close to the ear all bring bleed back.

| Take (silent) | Average level |
|---|---|
| Speakers | ______ dBFS |
| Headphones | ______ dBFS |
| Headphones, loud / one side off | ______ dBFS |

Every studio records vocals and overdubs in headphones for this reason. More on headphones and the cue mix:
[Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones](rec-monitoring.qmd); on bleed between instruments in one room:
[Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase](rec-placement.qmd).

## Monitoring and latency

**🎧 Monitor** sends the microphone through the Voice track so you hear yourself in the headphones, as a DAW's
**input monitoring** does. Two things to notice:

- **Only with headphones.** Monitoring through speakers sends the mic to the speakers, back into the mic, round and round: **feedback**, a howl.
- You hear yourself a little **late**. Sound takes time to go through the computer and back out: **latency**, here
  shown in milliseconds. Over about 10 ms it starts to feel odd; over 30 ms it's hard to sing with. Audio interfaces have
  **direct monitoring** (the mic straight to the headphones, before the computer) to get round it.

Latency also makes recordings land late on the timeline. The DAW moves each take earlier by the measured amount: the
**Latency fix** box in the editor. Set it to 0 on a take and look at the waveform: everything has slid late against the grid.

## Why phone calls don't sound like this

Video-call apps and voice memos run **echo cancellation**: they subtract what the speakers played from what the mic heard.
It's good for calls and bad for music (it chews up singing and room sound), so this DAW, like every real one, switches it off and
records exactly what the microphone hears.

## Tips for a clean take

- Headphones on, **closed-back** if you have them. The click quieter than you think.
- Point the microphone **away from** the headphones and the speakers; get close to the mic.
- Record a few seconds of the room in silence: you will hear what noise is there before it is under your voice.
- Watch the input meter: peaks around −10 dBFS, never in the red.

## In other DAWs

<div class="daw-map">

| | BandLab | Ableton Live | Logic Pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| Make an audio track | New track → Voice/Audio | Create → Insert Audio Track | Add Tracks (**Option+Cmd+N**) → Audio → Mic or Line |
| Choose the input | The track's input | The track's input chooser (View → In/Out) | Audio Input in the New Tracks dialog |
| Arm and record | Select the track, **R** | Arm the track, Arrangement Record (**F9**) | Select the track, **R** |
| Input monitoring | On Voice/Audio, Guitar and Bass tracks | Monitor: In / **Auto** (the default) / Off | Input Monitoring button (**I**) on the track |
| Latency fix | The latency test ([Fixing latency](https://help.bandlab.com/hc/en-us/articles/115002959414-Fixing-Latency)) | Settings → Audio → Driver Error Compensation (monitor Off) | Settings → Audio → Devices: I/O Buffer Size; Record → Low Latency Mode |
| Input level | Track meter while armed | Track meter while armed | Channel strip meter while armed |

</div>
